data.content_ref: inline:The target's own chosen analogy—natural selection—undermines its central claim that the preference is non-inductive. In biological natural selection, preferring the 'fittest' organism as a basis for future expectations is rational only under an assumption of environmental continuity: traits that were adaptive in the past are preferred precisely because we expect the environment to remain roughly stable. If the fitness landscape could change arbitrarily, past survival would carry no weight for future preference. The target explicitly frames corroboration as 'a strategic selection of the theory that has survived the most severe attempts at falsification' and calls the survivor 'currently the fittest candidate for further testing.' But calling something 'fittest for further testing' already presupposes that the testing environment (i.e., nature) will exhibit enough continuity that past falsification-resistance remains informative going forward. This is the uniformity-of-nature assumption—and it is inductive. The target therefore does not merely 'cost' the scientist probabilistic safety; it covertly relies on the very inductive premise it denies. Without this smuggled premise, the strategic preference is no more rational than preferring a theory at random, since there would be no reason to think past corroboration bears on future test performance. The target's claim that the preference is 'non-inductive' is thus internally incoherent given its own explanatory analogy.
